meta.name: Steel
meta.definition: The steel industry covers the mining of iron ore and coal, and the production, processing and distribution of crude and finished steel products (flat, long, structural, specialty) used across construction, infrastructure, automotive, engineering, packaging and consumer goods.

key_takeaways: India's finished steel consumption hit 163.7 MT in FY26 (up 7.6% YoY) and crude steel production reached 168.4 MT, making FY26 the best-ever year for the sector
Construction & infrastructure dominates demand at roughly 65-68% of consumption, with engineering/packaging (~22%) and automobiles (~9%) next
India remains heavily import-dependent on coking coal (85-90% imported, mostly from Australia) even as it targets cutting this to 65% by 2030-31

summary.report_markdown:
## Market size and trajectory
India's finished steel consumption reached **163.7 million tonnes (MT) in FY2025-26**, up 7.6% year-on-year, while crude steel production hit **168.4 MT** and finished steel production **160.9 MT** — government sources describe FY26 as the best-ever year for the sector. This continues a multi-year climb: consumption grew from 100.17 MT in FY2019-20 to 163.7 MT in FY2025-26, a near-doubling in six years. Value-based market-size estimates vary widely by methodology (roughly USD 140-190 billion for 2025 across different trade-journal and consultancy sources), but the volume trend is consistent and strong. Industry and government targets point to crude steel capacity of 300 MT by 2030-31 (National Steel Policy 2017) and 500 MT by 2047, requiring roughly Rs 10 lakh crore (~USD 156 billion) of fresh investment.

## Segments
By end-use, **construction and infrastructure account for roughly 65-68% of steel consumption**, followed by engineering and packaging (~22%) and automobiles (~9%). By product form, flat steel holds a slightly larger share (~54%) than long/structural products, with structural steel alone around 33.6% of the product mix in 2025. By production route, the Blast Furnace-Basic Oxygen Furnace (BF-BOF) process still accounts for ~44-46% of output, though EAF/induction-furnace routes (used for ~70% of long steel) are growing faster on the back of rising scrap availability and a government scrap policy targeting doubled domestic ferrous-scrap supply by 2030. Regionally, the East (Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal) supplies over half of production, while West & Central India is the single largest consuming region (~35% share).

## Growth drivers and outlook
Growth is underpinned by record government capex (Rs 12.2 lakh crore budgeted for FY2026-27, more than 3x FY2019-20 levels), the National Infrastructure Pipeline, Bharatmala, PM Gati Shakti, metro-rail expansion (24+ cities, 1,036+ km) and housing schemes (4 crore+ houses sanctioned under PMAY). The PLI Scheme for Specialty Steel (three rounds, cumulative outlay over Rs 23,000 crore realised) is pushing India up the value curve into coated, electrical, alloy and high-strength steel. India's steel demand has consistently outpaced global demand — growing at a 6-8% CAGR versus roughly flat-to-declining global growth — and India was the only top-10 producer with double-digit volume growth in 2025.

## Value chain and India-specific risks
India has abundant iron ore (Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka) that supports near-total captive self-sufficiency for large integrated players, but is structurally short of quality coking coal — importing 55-90% of requirements (mostly from Australia, with rising volumes from Russia, the US and Mozambique). This exposes producer margins to global coal-price swings and freight costs; the government's Mission Coking Coal aims to raise domestic output to 140 MT by FY2029-30 and cut import dependence from 85% to 65% by 2030-31. On the trade side, India has swung between net-importer and net-exporter status multiple times since FY2020 — becoming a net importer again in April-July FY27 — reflecting both China's steel oversupply (Chinese exports priced USD 50-100/tonne below domestic Indian steel) and currency/duty dynamics. In response, the government imposed a 12% provisional (later 3-year, tapering) safeguard duty on non-alloy/alloy flat steel products from April 2025, alongside Quality Control Orders (QCOs, 143 covering 723 products) and a 'melt and pour' domestic-manufacture rule to curb low-quality/dumped imports.

## Players and competitive landscape
The market is moderately consolidated: Tata Steel, JSW Steel and SAIL together hold roughly 45% share, with JSW Steel the largest private producer (targeting 50 MTPA by 2030, backed by over Rs 2 lakh crore of announced investment) and SAIL the largest state-owned integrated producer (~19-21 MT capacity). Other significant players include Jindal Steel & Power (JSPL), AM/NS India (ArcelorMittal-Nippon Steel JV building a new 7 MTPA plant in Andhra Pradesh), RINL/Vizag Steel, Jindal Stainless, APL Apollo Tubes, Bhushan Power & Steel and JTL Industries. Sector-wide capex plans point to a multi-year investment cycle exceeding Rs 9 lakh crore (~USD 100 billion) to hit the 2030 capacity target.

## Margins and profitability
Profitability across listed players peaked around FY22 and has since been under pressure from soft steel prices, high coking-coal costs and rising imports; EBITDA/tonne for most large players in FY24-25 remained well below FY22 peaks. JSPL has generally posted the best margins among peers owing to raw-material integration, while SAIL has lagged with the lowest EBITDA/tonne due to a higher share of low-value semis output. Analysts expect a margin recovery from FY26 onward on steel-price stabilisation, safeguard-duty support, and a rising share of value-added products (VAP shares have risen across Tata Steel, JSW, SAIL and JSPL, most already above 50% VAP mix).

sections.heading: Executive summary
prose: India is now the world's second-largest steel producer and consumer. In FY2025-26, crude steel production hit 168.4 million tonnes and finished steel consumption reached 163.7 million tonnes, making it the best-ever year for the sector.

Growth is being driven by government infrastructure spending, urbanisation, automotive expansion and large capacity build-outs by major producers. At the same time, India remains heavily dependent on imported coking coal, and cheap Chinese steel exports keep pressuring prices, prompting the government to impose a safeguard duty on flat steel imports in 2025.
The government has set targets of 300 million tonnes of capacity by 2030-31 and 500 million tonnes by 2047, positioning steel as a long-term growth sector backed by policy support.

sections.heading: Market size & growth
prose: Finished steel consumption in India reached 163.7 million tonnes in FY2025-26, up from 152.1 million tonnes the year before. This continues a steady multi-year climb: consumption stood at 100.2 million tonnes in FY2019-20, dipped to 94.9 million tonnes in FY2020-21 during the pandemic, and has risen every year since, reaching 105.8 million tonnes (FY2021-22), 119.9 million tonnes (FY2022-23) and 136.3 million tonnes (FY2023-24) before the latest jump.

The consistent year-on-year growth, capped by FY2025-26 being called the best-ever year for the sector, reflects sustained demand from construction, infrastructure and manufacturing, alongside expanding domestic production capacity.

sections.heading: Segments
prose: Construction and infrastructure dominate steel demand, accounting for about 65-68% of total consumption. Engineering and packaging make up around 22%, and the automobile industry contributes roughly 9%. By product type, flat steel (HR coils, CR coils, GP/GC sheets, plates) leads with 54.2% of the market, while structural steel holds 33.6%.

On the production side, the Blast Furnace-Basic Oxygen Furnace (BF-BOF) route remains dominant, accounting for 46.12% of 2025 output, even as electric arc furnace (EAF) capacity grows. Regionally, estimates vary by source: one puts West & Central India as the largest consuming region at 34.7% share, driven by manufacturing and automotive clusters, while another source cites North India as the largest region at about 31.78%.

sections.heading: Value chain
prose: The steel value chain starts with raw material sourcing. Iron ore is largely mined captively in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Karnataka, giving integrated players like Tata Steel and SAIL a cost advantage since they have near-100% captive access. Coking coal is a weak point: 80-90% is imported, mostly from Australia, exposing producers to global price swings.

Crude steel is produced either through the BF-BOF route, favoured by large integrated players with captive raw materials, or through EAF/induction furnace routes using scrap and sponge iron (DRI). India is the world's largest DRI producer, with about 63 million tonnes of capacity, and is largely self-sufficient in this feedstock.

Midstream processing converts crude steel into finished products through hot rolling, cold rolling and coating. Specialty lines such as electrical steel, tinplate and galvanized coils are being expanded under government incentive schemes, and these higher-value products carry better margins than commodity long products.

Distribution runs through direct sales, steel service centers, and dealer networks. SAIL, for example, has more than 2,300 dealers, with dealer margins typically capped by agreement at around Rs 1,200 per tonne over procurement price.

sections.heading: Distribution & channels
prose: Finished steel reaches customers through four main channels: direct sales, steel service centers, distributors and dealers, and online platforms. Direct sales and dealer networks remain the backbone of distribution for large producers, while online channels are an emerging but smaller route to market.

sections.heading: Key players & positioning
prose: Tata Steel, JSW Steel and SAIL together control about 45% of the domestic market. Tata Steel is India's largest producer with international operations in Europe and Thailand, and plans to double its domestic capacity from 21 million tonnes to 40 million tonnes by FY30. JSW Steel is India's largest private-sector producer, with capacity near 28-37.7 million tonnes and a target of 50 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) by 2030, backed by over Rs 2 lakh crore of planned investment. SAIL, the largest state-owned producer, runs five integrated plants with about 19-21.4 million tonnes of capacity, but is expected to see its market share fall below 10% by FY30 as private players grow faster.

Other notable players include Jindal Steel & Power (JSPL), expected to become India's fourth-largest steel manufacturer by FY26 after completing its Angul expansion; AM/NS India, a joint venture between ArcelorMittal and Nippon Steel building a new 7 MTPA mill in Andhra Pradesh; and Rashtriya Ispat Nigam (RINL/Vizag Steel), the second-largest public-sector steelmaker and India's largest rail supplier.

Downstream and specialty players include Jindal Stainless, a leading stainless steel maker in India and globally; APL Apollo Tubes, a leading structural steel tube and pipe maker with Rs 17,933 crore in trailing sales; and JTL Industries, a smaller tube maker expanding capacity from 0.6 to 1 MTPA with above-peer margins. NMDC Steel, recently demerged from NMDC, is building a new greenfield plant at Nagarnar. Consolidation has also shaped the sector: JSW Steel acquired Bhushan Power & Steel for Rs 19,700 crore via the insolvency process, and Essar Steel was acquired by ArcelorMittal and Nippon Steel to form AM/NS India.

sections.heading: Supply & capacity
prose: India's national crude steel capacity stood at 220.4 million tonnes in 2026, with capacity utilisation running at about 80%. Among major producers, JSW Steel's planned capacity is 37.7 million tonnes by FY26, Tata Steel's domestic capacity is 35.3 million tonnes (2024), SAIL's is 21.4 million tonnes (2024), and JSPL's planned capacity is 15.9 million tonnes by FY26.
The government is targeting 300 million tonnes of national capacity by 2030-31, meaning substantial further capacity additions are planned across all major producers over the next several years.

sections.heading: Tailwinds vs headwinds
prose: India was the only top-10 steel producer to post double-digit volume growth in 2025, while China, Japan and the EU stagnated or declined. This is backed by strong policy support: the National Steel Policy targets 300 million tonnes of capacity by 2030-31 and 500 million tonnes by 2047. Trade data also shows improvement, with steel exports up 29.1% year-on-year in March 2026 while imports fell 9.5%. A 12% safeguard duty on flat steel imports, imposed in April 2025, protects domestic producers from cheap or dumped imports, and India's abundant iron ore reserves, with potential output of 700 million tonnes a year, give integrated players a raw-material cost edge.

On the other hand, India imports 80-90% of its coking coal, mostly from Australia, exposing producers to global price and currency risk. Chinese steel oversupply continues to pressure prices, with Chinese exports priced USD 50-100 per tonne below Indian domestic steel. India's per-capita steel consumption, at roughly 93-98 kg, remains far below the global average of about 209-230 kg, limiting near-term demand upside per person. SAIL and other lower-tier producers face margin pressure and market-share loss to faster-growing private players. High logistics costs, at 13-14% of GDP, and the distance between eastern India's plants and demand centres add to delivered costs. Notably, India briefly slipped back into net-importer status during April-July FY27, as imports rose 36.6% year-on-year, outpacing 35% export growth.

sections.heading: Outlook
prose: India's steel sector enters its next phase from a position of strength: FY2025-26 was its best-ever year, with consumption at 163.7 million tonnes and production at 168.4 million tonnes. Growth is underpinned by a large government capex pipeline (Rs 12.2 lakh crore for FY2026-27), rising urbanisation, automotive sector expansion toward EVs, and aggressive capacity build-outs from Tata Steel, JSW Steel, SAIL and JSPL, all aimed at reaching the government's 300 million tonne target by 2030-31 and 500 million tonnes by 2047.

The main risks to this outlook are structural: heavy reliance on imported coking coal, persistent pressure from cheap Chinese exports, and India's low per-capita steel use relative to the rest of the world. The safeguard duty imposed in 2025 and the government's push to cut coking coal import dependence to 65% by 2030-31 both aim to address these vulnerabilities, but the sector's recent flip into net-importer territory during April-July FY27 shows the trade balance remains sensitive to global conditions.
